title: Application of separation techniques
competency: Compare and evaluate ways of separating mixtures used in the community.

keywords.def: Letting the solid in a liquid settle to the bottom.
Separating the parts of a mixture by physical methods, using differences in their physical properties.

en.text: Separation techniques are used every day. Filtration makes river water drinkable and separates honey from its comb. Evaporation gives salt from sea water. Distillation makes drinks like areki. Magnets sort iron and steel from glass and plastic. Sedimentation then decantation gives clear coffee and tella.

screens.title: Areki
screens.ask: Which method is used to make areki?
screens.after:
Areki is made by distillation.
The fermented mash is heated. The alcohol boils first, at a lower temperature than water.
The vapour is cooled and condensed. The collected liquid is areki.

screens.title: 2.5.2 Application of separation techniques
screens.ask: Tap each process to see where we use it.
items: Making river water potable (safe to drink); separating honey from its comb.
Getting common salt from sea water on a large scale.
Making drinks such as whisky, gin, brandy and areki.
Separating iron and steel from glass, plastic and aluminium.

screens.title: Project work: separation with local materials
steps: A beaker holds table salt, sulfur powder and iron filings.
Hint: sulfur and iron are insoluble in water; salt dissolves.
1. Pass a magnet in a plastic bag over the dry mixture to remove the iron.
2. Stir the rest in water: the salt dissolves.
3. Filter through a cloth: sulfur stays behind.
4. Leave the filtrate in the sun: the salt is left.

screens.title: Key words
defs: Letting the solid in a liquid settle to the bottom.
Separating the parts of a mixture by physical methods, using differences in their physical properties.

screens.text: Name the method used in industry: common salt is obtained from sea water on a large scale by …
screens.why:
In sea water, the salt is dissolved.
A dissolved solid is separated by evaporation.
The water evaporates in the sun and the salt is left.
A magnet, a sieve or decanting cannot remove dissolved salt.
screens.clue: Which method leaves the dissolved solid?

screens.why:
Honey from its comb: the wax comb stays on the cloth → filtration.
Salt from sea water: the water evaporates → evaporation.
Areki: alcohol vapour is condensed → distillation.
Iron from plastic waste: iron is magnetic → magnetic separation.
Clear tella: solids settle, the drink is poured off → sedimentation then decantation.
screens.clue: Think about what is being separated.
screens.text: Match each everyday use to the separation process (Table 2.5).
True or false? Filtration is a key step in making tap water safe to drink.
screens.why:
River water carries mud and other insoluble bits.
Filtration removes these solids.
The book says filtration makes river water potable and helps purify tap water. True.

screens.text: Project work: why must the magnet be used BEFORE adding water?
opts: Iron is easiest to remove from the dry mixture; wet filings stick and may rust
The order does not matter at all
screens.ans: Iron is easiest to remove from the dry mixture; wet filings stick and may rust
screens.why:
In the dry mixture, iron filings move freely to the magnet.
Wet filings stick to the other solids and may start to rust.
So the magnet goes first, while the mixture is dry.
The same order is used in Review Exercise Q15. Salt is never magnetic.

items.text: Exercise 2.8 I Q1 a: how would you separate a salt solution?
items.why:
The salt is dissolved in the water.
Evaporate the water: the salt is left.
To keep the water too, use distillation and collect the condensed vapour.
A magnet, sieve or separating funnel cannot remove dissolved salt.

items.text: Exercise 2.8 I Q1 b: how would you separate common salt and sand?
items.why:
Step 1: dissolve. Salt dissolves in water; sand does not.
Step 2: filter off the sand.
Step 3: evaporate the filtrate to get the salt.

items.text: Exercise 2.8 I Q1 c: how would you separate iron and charcoal?
items.why:
Iron is magnetic; charcoal is not.
A magnet pulls out the iron, the charcoal stays.
So use magnetic separation.

items.text: Exercise 2.8 I Q1 d: how would you separate oil, water and sand?
opts: Filter off the sand, then separating funnel
items.ans: Filter off the sand, then separating funnel
items.why:
Step 1: filter. The insoluble sand stays on the filter paper.
Step 2: pour the oil and water into a separating funnel. They form two layers.
Step 3: run off the lower water layer, then collect the oil.

items.title: Q2. Name the technique in each picture
pairs: A. Dish heated over a burner, steam rising
B. Magnet with iron filings above sand
C. Pear-shaped funnel with a tap
D. Sieve: large particles stay, fine earth falls
E. Coffee filter holding grounds over a jug
F. Pile of mixed coloured sweets
items.why:
Look for the tool in each picture.
A: heat and steam → evaporation. B: magnet → magnetic separation.
C: funnel with a tap → separating funnel. D: sieve → sieving.
E: filter holding grounds → filtration. F: sweets picked apart → separation by hand.
items.clue: Look for the tool in each picture.
items.text: Exercise 2.8 Q2: match each picture to the separation technique it shows.

pairs: Pouring clear coffee from the jebena
Drying wet grain in the sun
items.why:
Muddy water left to stand: the mud settles → sedimentation.
Pouring clear coffee off the grounds → decantation.
Straining tella through a cloth: the cloth holds back the solids → filtration.
Drying grain in the sun: the water escapes as vapour → evaporation.
items.text: Activity 2.19: match each job at home to the separation process it uses.

test.text: Where is distillation used? Distillation is used in the preparation of …
test.why:
Distillation boils a liquid and condenses the vapour.
Areki is made this way: the alcohol is boiled off and condensed.
Coffee and tella use sedimentation and decantation. Honey uses filtration.

test.text: True or false? Separating honey from its comb uses filtration.
test.why:
The honey passes through a cloth or filter.
The wax comb stays behind, like a residue.
Table 2.5 lists this as filtration. True.

test.text: Which separation steps do homemade coffee and tella use?
test.why:
Step 1: let it stand. The solids settle at the bottom: sedimentation.
Step 2: pour off the clear drink: decantation.
No magnet, boiling-off or sieve is needed.

test.text: Choose a method: a recycling centre wants to remove steel cans from plastic bottles. Which method?
test.why:
Steel contains iron, so it is magnetic.
Plastic is not magnetic.
A big magnet lifts out the steel cans.
So use magnetic separation (Table 2.5).

test.text: Plan the first step: table salt, sulfur powder and iron filings are mixed. Which is the right first step?
opts: Remove the iron with a magnet
test.ans: Remove the iron with a magnet
test.why:
Only iron is magnetic.
Remove it first with a magnet, while the mixture is dry.
Then dissolve the salt, filter off the sulfur, and evaporate the filtrate.
Evaporating, distilling or decanting first would not separate the solids.

notes.text: Exercise 2.8 I Q1 e (nitrogen and oxygen) needs fractional distillation of liquid air, which the book does not teach. Left out.
Exercise 2.8 Q2 picture F shows only mixed sweets; "separation by hand" is the intended answer by elimination.
The pictures of Exercise 2.8 Q2 are described in words.
